common_name: Lady Baltimore Hardy Hibiscus (Classic Clear Pink Red-Eyed Dinner-Plate Perennial)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Lady Baltimore is the classic mid-20th-century pink-flowered counterpart introduced alongside Lord Baltimore, bearing huge ruffled clear-pink blooms with a deep crimson eye.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply through summer since this wetland-edge hybrid wilts fast in dry spells. Lady Baltimore has been grown since the mid-1900s as the pink partner to the red-flowered Lord Baltimore, producing crepey, ruffled clear-pink flowers up to 8-9 inches across with a bold crimson-red central eye, opening in succession from midsummer into fall on a tall, well-branched clump. Like other hardy hibiscus it collapses to bare ground with the first hard frost and re-emerges quite late the following spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown. It is largely trouble-free in consistently damp soil, though Japanese beetles and occasional sawfly larvae can chew foliage where populations are heavy.

common_name: Anne Arundel Hibiscus (Compact Rose-Pink Red-Eyed Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Anne Arundel is an older Fleming hybrid hardy hibiscus valued for its compact habit and heavy set of rose-pink, red-eyed flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, keeping the root zone consistently damp through the growing season. Anne Arundel is a long-grown hybrid selection prized for staying noticeably more compact and floriferous than many older hardy hibiscus, bearing a heavy succession of 6-8 inch, clear rose-pink flowers centered with a deep red eye against mid-green foliage. Its shorter, sturdier habit makes it less prone to flopping than taller dinner-plate types, and it holds up well toward the front or middle of a mixed perennial border. As with all hardy hibiscus, it dies to the ground each winter and breaks dormancy late in spring, so mark its planting spot and be patient before assuming it has died.

common_name: Airbrush Effect Hibiscus (White with Pink Brushstroke-Patterned Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Airbrush Effect is a Summerific series cultivar whose white petals are streaked with soft pink brushstrokes radiating out from a rose-red center.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Airbrush Effect bears enormous, 8-9 inch white flowers overlaid with soft pink brushstroke streaks that fan outward from a small rose-red eye, giving each bloom a hand-painted, watercolor look against clean mid-green foliage. It keeps a noticeably more compact, rounded habit than many older dinner-plate hibiscus, making it easier to place in a mixed border, and produces a steady parade of single-day flowers from midsummer into fall. It dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and watch for Japanese beetles on foliage and flowers.

common_name: Summer Storm Hibiscus (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Lavender-Pink Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Summer Storm is a tall Summerific series cultivar pairing near-black purple foliage with large lavender-pink flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through the growing season since this wetland-edge hybrid wilts quickly if it dries out. Summer Storm is one of the tallest and darkest-leaved Summerific introductions, holding deep purple-black foliage on sturdy stems that support huge, 8-9 inch lavender-pink flowers with a small dark eye, opening in continuous succession from midsummer into fall. Its height and dramatic dark foliage make it a strong back-of-border anchor or focal point, contrasting sharply against green-leaved neighbors. Like other hardy hibiscus, it collapses to bare ground at first hard frost and resprouts quite late the following spring, so mark its location and cut old stems down before new growth begins.
